 Federal budget proposes changes to retirement savings and tax rules
 Eric Hattum, 
 DiscoverMooseJaw.com | 
 Saturday, Nov 14 2026, 5:00 AM 
 Share: 
 Copied! 
 Article continues below advertisement ↴ 
 Proposed changes to retirement savings and tax rules in the recent federal budget could simplify financial planning for retirees, farmers and business owners, according to a local accounting professional.
 Brad Stevenson, owner of Stevenson Accounting, said several measures outlined in the budget could affect how Canadians manage their retirement savings and tax obligations in the coming years.
 Among the proposals is a new RRSP for Life option, which would combine key features of a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) and a registered retirement income fund (RRIF).
 Under the proposed changes, individuals would no longer be required to convert their RRSP into a RRIF when they turn 71. However, minimum withdrawal requirements would still apply after age 71. 
 Proposed changes aim to simplify retirement planning
 Stevenson said the proposed RRSP for Life could reduce administrative requirements for retirees, particularly those with surviving spouses.
 “The immediate benefit is really limited because nothing's changed yet,” Stevenson said. “However, longer term, this is really about simplification. So we're getting rid of some of the red tape and the administration for retirees.”
 He noted that RRIF withdrawals are currently eligible for the pension income tax credit and pension income splitting provisions for individuals aged 65 and older, while RRSP withdrawals are not.
 Stevenson said he expects those provisions could be extended to RRSPs under the proposed legislation, although that remains to be confirmed. 
 He emphasized that the changes are not necessarily intended to provide a tax break, but rather to make retirement savings and withdrawals easier to manage.
 Farm rollover provisions and tax deadlines also targeted
 Other proposed budget measures include expanding farm rollover provisions to allow qualifying transfers to nieces, nephews, grandnieces and grandnephews.
 Stevenson said the expanded provisions would apply to qualifying transfers made after Jan. 1, 2027.
 The budget also proposes changes to individual tax filing deadlines, including moving the filing deadline for individuals and self-employed Canadians to May 15, beginning in spring 2028.
 Another proposed change would increase the threshold for required tax instalment payments from $3,000 to $7,500, also beginning in 2028. 
 Stevenson advises taxpayers to wait for further details
 Despite the proposed changes, Stevenson said taxpayers should not make immediate adjustments to their financial plans based solely on the budget announcements.
 “Not this year,” he said. “People shouldn't be changing their plans based on this headline alone.”
 He noted that a consultation period is still required, with the current process scheduled to conclude in January 2027. Implementation dates for the proposed measures have not yet been established.
 Local accounting services help connect retirement and business planning
 Stevenson said his firm works with individuals, farmers and business owners to connect retirement savings with their spending needs and overall tax planning. 
 For farmers and business owners, cash management can be an important part of preparing for retirement while maintaining enough money to support ongoing business expenses.
 He said Stevenson Accounting works alongside clients and their investment advisers to bring those financial considerations together and help develop a plan that meets their needs.
